entry: Perceptual phenomenon in which stimulation of one sensory or cognitive pathway involuntarily triggers experience in another. Synesthetes may perceive letters or numbers as inherently [[Color|colored]], or associate sounds with colors. Projective synesthesia involves seeing colors or shapes when stimulated; associative synesthesia involves a strong, involuntary link between a stimulus and the sense it triggers. The earliest recorded case is attributed to [[John Locke]], who in 1690 described a blind man who experienced the color scarlet on hearing a trumpet, though there is disagreement whether Locke described true synesthesia or a metaphor.

Mixture of [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] and [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]] in varying ratios, used mainly to produce [[Ammonia|ammonia]] or [[Methanol|methanol]]. Syngas (synthesis gas) is formed by steam reforming or partial oxidation of [[Natural gas|natural gas]] or liquid hydrocarbons, or by coal gasification. Coal-derived syngas typically contains 30 to 60% carbon monoxide, 25 to 30% hydrogen, 5 to 15% carbon dioxide and 0 to 5% methane. It has less than half the energy density of natural gas and is combustible, so it can serve as a fuel. Uses include reducing [[Iron ore|iron ore]] to sponge iron and making liquid fuels by the Fischer–Tropsch process. In November 2014 [[Audi]] opened a pilot plant, with Sunfire, to generate e-diesel from syngas made by high-temperature electrolysis.

South Korean politician and independence activist, first president of South Korea, 1948–60. Born in Hwanghae Province, Rhee was imprisoned in 1899 for activism and then studied in the United States, where he met presidents [[Theodore Roosevelt]] and [[Woodrow Wilson]]. He led the Korean Provisional Government in exile, based in [[Shanghai]], until his [[Impeachment|impeachment]] in 1925. Elected president of the Republic of Korea by the National Assembly in 1948, he governed through an administration characterized by [[Authoritarianism|authoritarianism]] and heavy reliance on US aid. He was president during the [[Korean War]] and refused to sign the armistice. After his 1956 reelection he pushed to remove the two-term limit from the constitution. In 1960, the opposition rejected his ally's vice-presidential victory as rigged, and the student-led April Revolution forced his resignation. He spent the rest of his life in exile in [[Honolulu]], Hawaii.

Branch of linguistics concerned with how words and morphemes combine into phrases and sentences. Central concerns include word order, grammatical relations, hierarchical sentence structure (constituency), agreement, and the relationship between structure and [[Semantics|meaning]]. Over 85% of languages usually place the subject first, in SVO or SOV order. Diverse approaches, including generative grammar and functional grammar, model the mental grammars that form and interpret sentences. The Aṣṭādhyāyī of [[Pāṇini]], from c. 4th century BC, is often cited as an early work approaching the sophistication of modern syntactic theory. The English term, which first appeared in 1548, derives partly from [[Ancient Greek]] and Latin. In logic, syntax is the study of how symbol strings form well-formed formulas in [[Formal language|formal languages]].

[[Electronic musical instrument]] that generates audio signals, typically by subtractive, additive or frequency modulation synthesis. Filters, envelopes and low-frequency oscillators shape the sound, and synthesizers are played with keyboards or controlled by sequencers and other instruments, often via MIDI. The Moog synthesizer, first sold in 1964, pioneered voltage-controlled oscillators, envelopes, filters and sequencers. The smaller, cheaper Minimoog (1970) standardized self-contained instruments with built-in keyboards. Wendy Carlos's *Switched-On Bach* (1968) brought synthesizers to the mainstream. Sampling, introduced with the Fairlight in 1979, influenced electronic and [[Hip-hop|hip hop]] music. The Yamaha DX7, released in 1983, was the first popular digital synthesizer. Synthesizers are now used in nearly every genre.

[[Chemical element]] that does not occur naturally on Earth, created by human manipulation of particles in a [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactor]], a [[Particle accelerator|particle accelerator]] or an atomic bomb explosion. The 24 synthetic elements, with atomic numbers 95–118, were first created between 1944 and 2010. All are unstable, and the half-lives of their longest-lived isotopes range from microseconds to millions of years. Six elements first made artificially, including [[Technetium|technetium]], created in 1937, were later found in trace quantities in nature. [[Plutonium]], first synthesized in 1940, has the largest atomic number of any element found in nature, though only in tiny quantities. It is known mainly for its use in atomic bombs and nuclear reactors. Elements with atomic numbers above 99 have no uses beyond scientific research, because their half-lives are extremely short.

[[Sexually transmitted infection]] caused by the [[Bacteria|bacterium]] *Treponema pallidum* subspecies *pallidum*. Symptoms depend on the stage: primary, secondary, latent or tertiary. The primary stage typically presents as a single painless chancre, a skin ulcer; secondary syphilis causes a diffuse rash, often on the palms and soles. Latent syphilis may cause no symptoms for years, while tertiary disease can involve gummas, neurological problems or heart symptoms. Infection is most often spread by sexual contact, and mothers can transmit it to babies during [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]] or birth. Diagnosis usually relies on [[Blood test|blood tests]]. The risk of spread can be reduced with a latex or polyurethane [[Condom|condom]]. Syphilis is treated with [[Penicillin]] or other [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]]; [[Doxycycline]] is used for people with a severe penicillin allergy. In 2015 about 45.4 million people had infections, and the disease caused about 107,000 deaths, down from 202,000 in 1990.

River in [[Central Asia]], historically known as the Jaxartes. It rises in the [[Tian Shan]] mountains of Kyrgyzstan and eastern Uzbekistan and flows 2,256.25 km (1,401.97 mi) west and northwest through Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and [[Kazakhstan]] to the northern remnants of the [[Aral Sea]]. It and the [[Amu Darya]] are the two main rivers of the Aral Sea's [[Endorheic basin|endorheic]] basin. Soviet-era irrigation diverted both rivers into farmland, which caused the virtual disappearance of the Aral Sea, once the world's fourth-largest lake. In 329 BC the army of [[Alexander the Great]] reached the river and fought the Battle of Jaxartes against the Saka nomads.

City and seat of Onondaga County in central [[New York (state)|New York]], United States. With 148,620 residents, it is the most populous city in Central New York. Established in 1820 and named for the classical Greek city of Syracuse on [[Sicily]], for its similar natural features, it produced commercial salt from brine springs into the late 19th century, earning the nickname "The Salt City." It was a major industrial center until the mid-20th century and is now a hub for higher education and services, home to Syracuse University. The [[Erie Canal]] has run through the city since the 1820s.

Ancient Greek city and comune on the southeastern coast of [[Sicily]], Italy (pop., 2026: 115,515). Founded by Corinthian colonists in 733 BC (by Thucydides' dating) on the island of Ortygia, Syracuse was the main rival of [[Carthage]] and rivaled [[Athens]] in power. It was the birthplace of the mathematician [[Archimedes]], who led its defense against the Roman siege of 212 BC. Syracuse was the de facto capital of the [[Byzantine Empire]] under Constans II from 663 to 668 and for centuries the capital of Sicily, until a 877–878 siege during the Aghlabid conquest led to its decline in favor of Palermo. Its historic center, Ortygia, took its [[Baroque]] form after a 1693 earthquake. In 1943 the Armistice of Cassibile, ending hostilities between the Kingdom of Italy and the Allies, was signed southwest of the city. [[UNESCO]] designated Syracuse, with the Necropolis of Pantalica, a World Heritage Site in 2005.

Country in [[West Asia]] on the eastern Mediterranean, officially the Syrian Arab Republic. [[Damascus]] is the capital and largest city, and the population is about 26 million. After centuries of [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] rule, Syria was a French mandate and gained de jure independence in 1945 and de facto independence in 1946. Coups were frequent until a 1963 coup established one-party rule by the Ba'ath Party. Hafez al-Assad came to power in 1970, and his son [[Bashar al-Assad]] succeeded him in 2000. The [[Syrian civil war]] began in 2011 and culminated in the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. [[Ahmed al-Sharaa]] was formally appointed president in January 2025. Levantine Arabs are the largest ethnic group and Sunni Muslims the largest religious group. The economy, once mainly agricultural, deteriorated after 2011, and the country has six UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

Armed conflict in [[Syria]] that began with protests in March 2011 and culminated in the [[Fall of the Assad regime|fall of the Assad regime]] in December 2024. Protests against the Ba'athist government of [[Bashar al-Assad]], part of the wider [[Arab Spring]], turned into war after government forces responded with lethal force and armed opposition groups, including the Free Syrian Army, formed. Iran and Russia supported Assad, while Qatar, Turkey and a United States-led program aided rebels. Chemical weapons, used mainly by government forces, were the deadliest such use since the [[Iran–Iraq War]]. From 2014 the [[Islamic State]] seized much of eastern Syria, and a U.S.-led coalition bombed it. In November 2024 a rebel offensive took Aleppo within three days, and Damascus fell on December 8 as Assad fled to [[Moscow]]. The war displaced more than 6 million people. In January 2025 the new government appointed [[Ahmed al-Sharaa]] president.

Simple reciprocating pump consisting of a plunger, or in modern syringes a piston, fitted within a cylindrical barrel, used to draw in or expel liquid or gas. Syringes are used in clinical medicine to administer injections, infuse intravenous therapy and measure or draw liquids. Hypodermic syringes, used with hypodermic needles, inject into or withdraw fluid from body tissues. Injecting air into a blood vessel can cause a hazardous air embolism, so air is expelled before an injection. Most modern medical syringes are plastic and single-use, reducing the spread of blood-borne disease. Reused syringes spread [[HIV]] and [[Hepatitis|hepatitis]] among [[Drug|intravenous drug]] users, and people with diabetes who reuse syringes for multiple daily [[Insulin|insulin]] injections risk serious infection. Common tip designs include the Luer lock, which twists on, and the slip tip.

Group of interacting or interrelated elements that act according to rules or constraints to form a unified whole. A system is described by its boundaries, structure and purpose, and is shaped by its environment. Most systems are open, exchanging matter and energy with their surroundings, like a car or the [[Earth|Earth]]. A closed system exchanges energy but not matter, and an isolated system exchanges neither; the [[Universe]] is a theoretical example of the last. [[Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot]] pioneered the concept of a system in natural science in the 19th century, studying the working substance of steam engines in [[Thermodynamics|thermodynamics]]. In the late 1940s and mid-1950s, Norbert Wiener and Ross Ashby developed [[Cybernetics]], the mathematical study of control and communication. The word derives from [[Latin]] systēma, itself from Greek.

Port city and capital of West Pomeranian Voivodeship in northwestern [[Poland]], historically known in English as Stettin (pop., 2022: 391,566). On the Oder River near the [[Baltic Sea]] and the German border, it is Poland's seventh-largest city. It was the capital of a duchy ruled by the [[Griffin|House of Griffin]] and later passed under Swedish and Prussian control. After [[World War II]] it became part of Poland under the Potsdam Agreement. In 1980 an agreement between protesters and the communist regime, signed in Szczecin, paved the way for the Solidarity movement. [[NATO]]'s Multinational Corps Northeast has been headquartered in the city since 1999.

American girl group formed in 1990 in [[Atlanta]], Georgia, best known with Tionne "T-Boz" Watkins, Lisa "Left Eye" Lopes and Rozonda "Chilli" Thomas. In the 1990s the group had nine top-ten hits on the Billboard Hot 100, including four number-one singles, among them "Creep" and "Waterfalls." Its album *CrazySexyCool* (1994) was certified diamond by the RIAA. TLC has sold over 60 million records and won five career [[Grammy Awards]]. After Lopes's death, the remaining members continued as a duo.

Trinitrotoluene, an [[Explosive|explosive]] compound prized for its convenient handling properties. German chemist Julius Wilbrand first synthesized it in 1863, using it as a yellow dye. Its explosive properties were discovered in 1891 by Carl Häussermann. It is so insensitive that in 1910 Britain exempted it from the Explosives Act, and the German armed forces adopted it for artillery shells in 1902. It is made from [[Toluene|toluene]] by three nitration steps using [[Sulfuric acid|sulfuric]] and [[Nitric acid|nitric acid]]. Its explosive yield is the standard comparison for bombs and asteroid impacts.

Convention for expressing the [[Energy|energy]] released in an explosion, defined by reference to [[TNT]]. One ton of TNT equivalent is defined as 4.184 gigajoules (1 gigacalorie), roughly the energy released by detonating a metric ton of TNT. The unit is routinely used for nuclear weapon yields. The 1945 [[Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki]] used bombs with yields of 15 and 20 kilotons respectively. The largest nuclear weapon ever tested, [[Tsar Bomba]], had a yield of 50 megatons. A kiloton of TNT can be visualized as a cube 8.46 m on a side.

[[Red dwarf]] star in the constellation Aquarius, about 40.66 light-years from Earth, with seven known [[Exoplanet|exoplanets]]. Its mass is about 9% of the [[Sun]]'s, and it is estimated to be 7.6 billion years old, older than the [[Solar System]]. The star's discovery was first published in 2000. Two terrestrial planets were found in 2016 and five more in 2017. All orbit in 1.5 to 19 days, are likely tidally locked, and lie in the same plane. Planets d, e, f and g orbit where liquid water may be possible, but there is no evidence of an atmosphere on any of the planets.

[[Taiwan|Taiwanese]] multinational [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] contract manufacturer, holding about 70% of the global foundry market. Founded in 1987 as a joint venture, it was the world's first dedicated chip foundry. Its customers include [[Nvidia]], Apple, [[Broadcom]], [[Qualcomm]] and [[AMD]]. It was the first foundry to produce 7-nanometer and 5-nanometer chips, and the first to use [[ASML]]'s extreme ultraviolet lithography in high volume. In 1997 it became the first Taiwanese company listed on the [[New York Stock Exchange]]. Its role as a supply-chain bottleneck raises concerns that a disruption could cause a worldwide chip shortage.

Soviet [[Tank|medium tank]] of [[World War II]], with a 76.2 mm gun more powerful than many contemporaries and 60-degree sloped armor. Its low cost and quick production meant German panzer forces often faced Soviet tank forces several times their size. German generals praised it during [[Operation Barbarossa]], and the Soviets built over 80,000 T-34s of all variants, the most-produced tank of the war. It suffered the most tank losses ever, with 44,900 lost or damaged. Its development led to the [[T-54/T-55]] series, the second most-produced tank of all time.

Series of Soviet medium tanks introduced after [[World War II]], and the most-produced tank in history, with estimated production of 96,500 to 100,000. Designed for ease of manufacture and simple operation by a largely conscript army, it became the main tank of Soviet armored units and [[Warsaw Pact]] armies from the late 1950s. Replaced in Soviet service by later models, it remains in use with up to 50 other armies. Its appearance in the West spurred the United Kingdom to develop the L7 gun and the United States to create the M60 tank.

British Army officer, archaeologist, diplomat and writer known for his role in the Arab Revolt against the [[Ottoman Empire]]. Before World War I he worked as an archaeologist for the [[British Museum]] at Carchemish in Ottoman Syria. After the war began in 1914 he was posted to the Arab Bureau, a British military intelligence unit in Egypt. He was assigned as liaison to Emir Faisal, a leader of the revolt, with the British Military Mission in the [[Hejaz]]. He took part in engagements culminating in the capture of Damascus in October 1918. After the war he worked with Faisal in the Foreign Office. In 1922 he withdrew from public life and served as an enlisted man in the Army and Royal Air Force until 1935. His account of the revolt, *Seven Pillars of Wisdom*, was published in 1926, and his fame owed much to the reporting of American journalist Lowell Thomas.

American-born British poet, essayist and playwright. Born in [[St. Louis]], Missouri, to a prominent Boston Brahmin family, he moved to the United Kingdom in 1914, became a British subject in 1927 and converted to [[Anglicanism]]. A leading figure of modernist poetry in English, he altered the art through his style, verse structure and pessimistic language. His early poem "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" (1915) was considered outlandish at its publication; it was followed by *The Waste Land* (1922), *The Hollow Men* (1925), *Ash Wednesday* (1930) and *Four Quartets* (1943). He wrote seven plays, including *Murder in the Cathedral* (1935) and *The Cocktail Party* (1949). He was awarded the 1948 Nobel Prize in Literature "for his outstanding, pioneer contribution to present-day poetry."

Last Sapa Inca of the Neo-Inca State, the final independent remnant of the [[Inca Empire]]. The Neo-Inca State was founded in Vilcabamba, in the Upper Amazon northeast of [[Cusco]], by members of the royal family after the Spanish conquest of Peru in the 1530s. Túpac Amaru succeeded his brothers as ruler there. The Spanish viceroy Francisco de Toledo declared war on April 14, 1572, and on June 24 Spanish forces entered Vilcabamba to find it deserted and destroyed. Túpac Amaru fled into the lowland forests with a small party. The Spanish pursued him for months, and he was executed after capture. His name derives from Quechua words meaning "royal" or "shining" and "snake."
